steps.title: Bring a solid into the scene
steps.goal: Create a kernel box, convert it to display data, and add it as one undoable scene object.
steps.trace: Kernel box → triangle extraction → validated display Mesh → document transaction → GPU upload → visible solid
steps.question: Why does a failed mesh conversion belong outside the GPU draw loop?
steps.answer: Conversion establishes the display data contract before an object enters the scene. A failure should leave the document and history unchanged. The draw loop should read already valid GPU resources; it cannot repair an invalid index or decide whether a failed document edit should be kept.
steps.story:
Create a grey box with the geometry kernel and adapt it to our validated display mesh. `to_render` supplies float vertices and triangle indices; the adapter selects position and colour for our six-float vertex layout.

The box has eight geometric corners, six quad faces and twelve triangles. This example handles its convex faces; imported concave faces need later topology work.

Convert kernel `u32` indices with `u16::try_from`. Return an error for an index that cannot fit rather than connecting the wrong corners.

Add `History::try_edit`: commit and clear redo only on success; restore the previous scene on error. A test deliberately mutates then fails. The box is unlit here; the next shader change reveals its face directions.

![A kernel box becomes a validated display mesh; a successful document transaction inserts it before the renderer uploads its triangles.](../illustrations/journey-17.svg)
steps.result: Type `Example Box`, then `View Isometric`. A solid box appears. `Undo` removes that one object; `Redo` restores it.
steps.experiment: Add a box and undo. In the rollback test, predict whether a failed new edit should erase the available redo. Run the test: it should not. Then redo the successful box addition. Separate three questions in your notes: did creation succeed, did the document change, and was the change uploaded?
steps.production: The final viewer converts kernel geometry into renderable lanes while preserving document identity and transactional edits. This adapter is the first real kernel-to-display connection; later lessons retain face and edge provenance and share allocations across many objects.
steps.browser_status: Kernel geometry becomes an undoable scene object.
steps.image_result: The new object is the pale grey box behind the triangles. Its faces have the same colour because lighting is not implemented yet. The helper adds a kernel box, uploads the scene, and checks its projected position and visible area.

steps.title: Read the shape through light
steps.goal: Shade the box faces according to their direction, using the same mesh and renderer.
steps.trace: World position → neighbouring surface directions → normal → light alignment → fragment colour
steps.question: Why should orbiting the camera leave the brightness of a particular box face unchanged?
steps.answer: Both the normal and the light direction are expressed in world coordinates. Orbit changes where we look from, not the face direction or the light. A different face may become visible, but the same face keeps the same brightness. Mixing a camera-space normal with a world-space light would break that relationship.
steps.story:
Shade the grey box according to surface direction. Pass world positions from the vertex shader to the fragment shader.

`dpdx` and `dpdy` estimate horizontal and vertical position changes. Their cross product gives the triangle normal; normalisation makes it unit length. Dot it with the unit world-space light direction to measure alignment.

Use `abs` for this display's two-sided lighting and retain a minimum brightness of 0.3. Multiply RGB before the existing sRGB output conversion.

Only shader logic changes. Mesh still supplies positions and colours, Camera positions the view, and Renderer submits the triangles. Adjoining box faces now have visibly different brightness.

![Two directions along a face give its normal; comparing that normal with the light controls brightness.](../illustrations/journey-18.svg)
steps.result: Type `Example Box` and `View Isometric`. Faces pointing in different directions should have different brightness, making the box’s shape easier to read.
steps.experiment: Change the light to vec3<f32>(0.0, 0.0, 1.0). Predict the box first: the top should be bright and both vertical sides equally dark. Try it, then restore the original light. Explain why this changes colour without moving a single vertex.
steps.production: This is flat lighting: each triangle has one surface direction. The final viewer also needs smooth normals, materials, two-sided surface rules and contact shadows. Those features will extend the same distinction between geometry, view and shading.
steps.browser_status: Surface direction changes brightness, not geometry.
steps.image_result: Compare the box with lesson 17: its left face is darker than its right face, and its top is brightest. Geometry and camera are unchanged; the shader now shades each face. Three projected face samples check those brightness levels.

edits.why: Pass world positions through the pipeline and turn face direction into brightness.
Report that lighting changes brightness without changing geometry.

steps.browser_caption: Compare the box with lesson 17: the same geometry now has three face brightnesses.

steps.title: Give application state one owner
steps.goal: Own scene, selection, camera, background and history in one browser-independent value.
steps.trace: Editor owns scene and history beside camera, background and selection
steps.story:
Editor owns application state. Action names an input; Change tells drawing whether scene data or only the view changed.

Keep History private so document edits follow one path. Default constructs an editor with the existing demonstration scene.

![Editor owns document and view state.](../illustrations/journey-direct-18a-editor.svg)
steps.result: Inspect the supplied state fixtures. Zooming the owned camera preserves the document IDs and empty selection.
steps.question: Why put these values in one struct?
steps.answer: An input handler can borrow one editor rather than manage separate captured scene, camera, selection and history values.
steps.experiment: Change the ownership test to pan the camera. Its scene IDs should still match; restore the original zoom check.
steps.production: The application owner keeps document and view lifetimes together while history stores document changes only.
steps.browser_status: Surface direction changes brightness, not geometry.
steps.browser_caption: Native checks establish the new state owner. Chrome independently retains the preceding lighting and typed-command path; browser routing moves into Editor in the final step.

edits.why: Declare the action names, change kinds and application owner. Check a camera change keeps document identity.
Make the editor available to both the browser and native checks.

steps.title: Apply document and view actions in Rust
steps.goal: Apply actions through one editor while preserving view settings during history and reset.
steps.trace: Action → Editor::apply → History for document edits → Change::Scene or Change::View
steps.story:
Editor::apply handles an Action and returns the kind of drawing change. Document edits use History; camera and background changes stay outside it.

Result propagates a failed add operation. After deletion or history travel, retain selection only if its ID still exists. View Reset keeps the current window aspect.

![Actions update the editor and report the drawing change.](../illustrations/journey-direct-18b-actions.svg)
steps.result: Inspect the supplied state fixtures. Undo removes the added box while keeping zoom and background; View Reset preserves the current aspect.
steps.question: Why return Change rather than redraw here?
steps.answer: The editor owns application values, not GPU objects. Its caller decides when to upload scene data and draw.
steps.experiment: Set camera aspect to 2.0 in the reset test. Reset distance and orientation should change while that aspect stays 2.0.
steps.production: Actions preserve the document/view boundary and describe the synchronization required. This checkpoint also retains aspect during reset before browser routing is introduced.
steps.browser_status: Surface direction changes brightness, not geometry.
steps.browser_caption: Native checks exercise the new action route and render its selected box. Chrome retains the earlier event handler and lighting result; the following step connects browser input to Editor.

edits.why: Implement the action route and check history preserves the view. Keep the current aspect when resetting the camera.

steps.title: Route browser input through the editor
steps.goal: Move document actions into a browser-independent editor while keeping picking, undo and drawing working.
steps.trace: Typed command or canvas click → Action → Editor::apply → Change → scene upload when required → draw
steps.question: Why does Change::View skip set_scene?
steps.answer: The scene data did not change. Redrawing with the editor camera or background is sufficient.
steps.story:
Convert submitted commands and canvas clicks to Action values. Apply them through Editor, upload only when Change is Scene, then redraw from the editor camera and background.

The closure captures one mutable editor. The GPU renderer keeps its derived representation separate from the document owner.

![Browser input uses the same editor route and drawing-change result.](../illustrations/journey-direct-19-actions.svg)
steps.result: Type Example Box, then Undo and Redo. The box disappears and returns through the editor route.
steps.experiment: Pan Right, delete a selected object and Undo. The document returns while the camera stays where you put it.
steps.production: The full command system will build on this boundary. commands, keyboard input and tools request document operations through the same owner, while rendering consumes the result. More commands should add behavior here or in focused command modules, not duplicate transactions in UI handlers.
steps.browser_status: Every document action follows the same editor path.
steps.image_result: The box is yellow because it is selected. The helper sends AddBox, Isometric and three SelectNext actions through Editor, then checks the selected pixels. This demonstrates the result of the shared action path; it does not prove that a typed browser command delivered those actions.

edits.why: Check selection repair, redo preservation and picking through the editor’s current camera.
